title: Doctors List Early Lung Cancer Warning Signs People Keep Overlooking
excerpt: A cough past three weeks, blood in sputum, repeated chest infections and unexplained weight loss should be checked, not waited out, oncologists and pulmonologists say.
body:
• A cough lasting more than three weeks, coughing up blood, repeated chest infections, unexplained weight loss and persistent breathlessness should be evaluated by a doctor, CARE Hospitals physicians say.
  • Fortis oncologist Dr Nitesh Rohatgi says a cough that persists four to five weeks or changes in character deserves re-evaluation, even if it was first blamed on allergy, pollution or a smoker's cough.
  • For readers in the US: the CDC says yearly low-dose CT screening is recommended only for adults aged 50 to 80 with a 20 pack-year or more smoking history who smoke now or quit within the past 15 years.
  • India recorded an estimated 1,12,659 new lung cancer cases and 98,687 deaths in 2024, according to GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates cited by CARE Hospitals doctors.

Lung cancer is often diagnosed late, not because early signs are absent, but because they are subtle, familiar and therefore ignored. That is the warning running through two sets of doctors' comments published for Lung Cancer Awareness Month, reported by Times Now and by physicians at CARE Hospitals writing in Healthwire Media.

The signs doctors say not to wait out

A persistent cough heads both lists. "Smokers often normalize chronic coughing, making it harder to recognize when something has changed. Any cough that persists for four to five weeks or alters in character deserves re-evaluation," said Dr Nitesh Rohatgi, Senior Director of Medical Oncology at Fortis Memorial Research Institute. Dr Sudheer Nadimpalli, Senior Consultant Interventional Pulmonologist at CARE Hospitals, Hitech City, puts the threshold at three weeks: a cough lasting more than three weeks, particularly with unexplained weight loss, chest pain or repeated chest infections, should be evaluated.

Blood-streaked sputum, even in tiny quantities, should never be ignored. Often blamed on throat irritation or infection, this symptom, called hemoptysis, can occur even in early lung cancer and requires prompt assessment, Rohatgi said. Gradually increasing breathlessness, wheezing or reduced exercise tolerance may result from partial airway obstruction caused by a tumour, he added, while a persistent hoarse voice may indicate involvement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Repeated episodes of bronchitis or pneumonia, especially in the same area of the lung, are another flag. "Temporary improvement with antibiotics should not end the investigation if infections keep returning," Rohatgi said. The CARE Hospitals list adds persistent chest pain, unexplained weight loss and fatigue that does not improve with rest. Both sets of doctors stress the same caveat: these symptoms do not necessarily mean cancer, and they occur in several other conditions, but persistent or worsening symptoms should be checked rather than self-diagnosed.

"I often tell patients, know your body the way you know your car. If your car makes an unusual noise and the mechanic says it's fine, but the noise persists, you don't ignore it — you go back. You insist. You ask again."

— Dr Nitesh Rohatgi, Senior Director of Medical Oncology, Fortis Memorial Research Institute

Why the delay happens

In India, the overlap with other diseases compounds the problem. When symptoms do appear, CARE Hospitals doctors note, they can resemble tuberculosis, asthma and chronic bronchitis. Smoking remains the biggest risk factor, Nadimpalli said, but it is not the only one: long-term exposure to air pollution, second-hand smoke and certain workplace hazards can also contribute, and people who have never smoked can develop the disease.

The scale is large. According to GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates released by the International Agency for Research on Cancer in July 2026 and cited by CARE Hospitals, India recorded an estimated 1,12,659 new lung cancer cases and 98,687 deaths in 2024, about 7.2 per cent of all new cancer cases and nearly 11 per cent of cancer-related deaths in the country. Dr Saadvik Raghuram Y, Director of Medical Oncology at CARE Hospitals, Banjara Hills, identifies delayed diagnosis as a major challenge, noting that detecting lung cancer earlier can provide more treatment options, including potentially curative treatment for suitable patients.

Screening is narrower than symptom-checking

Screening and symptom investigation are different routes. The CDC's lung cancer screening page says the recommended screening test is low-dose computed tomography, and that yearly screening is recommended only for adults at high risk: aged 50 to 80, with a 20 pack-year or more smoking history, who smoke now or have quit within the past 15 years. The CDC also notes screening carries risks, including false-positive results and overdiagnosis.

The practical takeaway from both sets of doctors is about persistence, not panic. A symptom that lasts beyond three to five weeks, keeps returning, or is getting worse is a reason to go back to a doctor and ask directly whether cancer has been ruled out. "If symptoms persist beyond four to five weeks, it is entirely reasonable to return to your doctor and ask the uncomfortable but vital question: 'Could this still be cancer?'" Rohatgi said.
nri_angle: US-based readers get the exact CDC low-dose CT screening criteria — age 50 to 80 and a 20 pack-year smoking history — alongside the symptom thresholds Indian specialists cite.
